triage.name: Kwashiorkor
triage.reason: Edematous protein-energy malnutrition with classic skin, hair and edema findings; a student can reach it from diet history and exam.

demographics: Most common in low- and middle-income countries in the tropics and subtropics
Occurs in settings of food insecurity, famine, or displacement
Can occur in any population where protein intake is severely inadequate

risk_factors.text: Weaning onto a starchy, protein-poor diet

chief_complaints.text: My child's feet and face are swollen
His hair is falling out and changing color
He is irritable and not himself

hpi.duration: Usually weeks to months at presentation
hpi.progression: Progressive swelling, poor growth, and skin and hair changes; may be precipitated by an infection
hpi.location: Generalized, with swelling of feet, legs, and face
hpi.quality: Pitting edema, skin may feel tight and shiny

associated_symptoms.text: Swelling of the feet and legs
Hair that is sparse, brittle, and depigmented
Skin that is dry, peeling, and hyperpigmented

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with failure to thrive and edema but less obvious hair and skin changes.
Rare, but can occur with severe protein restriction or malabsorption; edema and skin changes may be attributed to other causes.

general.mild: Alert but irritable, with mild pitting edema of the feet and lower legs
general.moderate: Irritable and apathetic, with obvious pitting edema of the legs, feet and face; sparse, brittle hair
general.severe: Apathetic and withdrawn, with marked generalized edema, peeling hyperpigmented skin and depigmented hair
general.critical: Lethargic or obtunded, with anasarca, extensive skin desquamation and signs of shock or severe infection

findings.maneuver: Press firmly over the dorsum of the foot and the lower leg for several seconds
findings.finding: Pitting edema of the feet and lower legs

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the face and periorbital area
findings.finding: Swelling of the face, often with puffy eyelids

findings.maneuver: Plot weight, length and head circumference on a growth chart
findings.finding: Weight and length below the expected percentiles for age

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the deltoid, quadriceps and gluteal muscles
findings.finding: Reduced muscle bulk with preserved subcutaneous fat

findings.maneuver: Inspect the legs, groin and pressure areas
findings.finding: Dry, peeling, hyperpigmented skin with a mosaic or 'crazy pavement' pattern

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin in sun-exposed and pressure areas
findings.finding: Patchy hyperpigmentation

findings.maneuver: Inspect the scalp hair and pull gently on a few strands
findings.finding: Sparse, brittle hair that is depigmented and easily plucked
Distended abdomen, sometimes with a palpable enlarged liver

findings.maneuver: Palpate the right upper quadrant below the costal margin
findings.finding: Enlarged, smooth, non-tender liver

findings.maneuver: Observe the child's interaction and response to the examiner
findings.finding: Apathetic, withdrawn and difficult to engage

findings.maneuver: Observe the child's behavior during the examination
findings.finding: Irritable and easily distressed

findings.maneuver: Inspect the sclera and skin in natural light
findings.finding: No yellow discoloration of the sclera or skin
No crackles or rales

findings.maneuver: Inspect the neck veins with the child at 45 degrees
findings.finding: No jugular venous distension

labs.caveat: Hypoalbuminemia is the key biochemical marker; it drives the edema and is often the most striking abnormality.
Low total protein reflects the protein deficit; it falls with albumin.
Normocytic or normochromic anemia is common; may be masked by hemoconcentration before rehydration.
Microcytosis suggests coexisting iron deficiency, which is common in this population.
Hypokalemia from diarrhea and poor intake; can be life-threatening and worsens with refeeding.
Hyponatremia is often dilutional from total body water excess; correct slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination.
Hypophosphatemia is common and can drop further with refeeding; monitor closely during nutritional rehabilitation.
Hypomagnesemia often accompanies hypokalemia and hypocalcemia; replace to correct the others.
Total calcium is low partly because albumin is low; check ionized calcium or correct for albumin.
Hypoglycemia is common and dangerous, especially in young children and with infection.
Low BUN from poor protein intake and reduced urea production.
Low creatinine reflects reduced muscle mass; a 'normal' creatinine can hide renal impairment.
Mild transaminase elevation from hepatic steatosis; marked elevation suggests another cause.
Mild elevation from fatty liver; usually less than AST.
May be elevated from hepatic involvement or coexisting rickets.
Prolonged PT from impaired hepatic synthesis of clotting factors; check INR before procedures.
Elevated INR reflects synthetic liver dysfunction; give vitamin K if bleeding or before procedures.
May be low from marrow suppression or high from concurrent infection; a normal count does not exclude serious infection.
Thrombocytopenia can occur with marrow suppression or sepsis.
Mild proteinuria can occur; heavy proteinuria suggests nephrotic syndrome rather than kwashiorkor.
Ketones are usually less prominent than in marasmus because some carbohydrate is still consumed.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia
Prolonged QT interval from hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia or hypocalcemia
Flattened T waves with prominent U waves from hypokalemia
ST depression or flattened T waves from hypokalemia
Premature atrial or ventricular beats from electrolyte derangement
Prolonged PR interval from hypocalcemia

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected hepatic steatosis or to assess liver size

findings.text: Diffusely increased hepatic echogenicity consistent with fatty infiltration

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected cardiac dysfunction or to exclude heart failure as a cause of edema

findings.text: Normal chamber size and systolic function
Reduced systolic function suggesting coexisting cardiomyopathy

initial.why: Assesses albumin, total protein, electrolytes, glucose, calcium and liver enzymes; hypoalbuminemia is central to the diagnosis
Looks for anemia, leukocytosis from infection, or cytopenias
Evaluates sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, glucose and renal function; guides fluid and electrolyte replacement
Hypomagnesemia is common and must be corrected to fix potassium and calcium
Hypophosphatemia is common and worsens with refeeding
Detects coagulopathy from impaired hepatic synthetic function
Baseline before any procedures and to assess liver function
Screens for proteinuria and urinary infection
Rules out pregnancy in any postmenarchal female before imaging or treatment decisions

confirmatory.why: Marked hypoalbuminemia in the setting of edema, poor growth and characteristic skin and hair changes confirms the diagnosis

supporting.why: Supports the diagnosis of a concurrent infection, which is common and often precipitates presentation
May be elevated with infection or inflammation
Evaluates iron deficiency, which is common in this population
supporting.only_if: microcytic anemia or suspected iron deficiency

supporting.why: Assesses hepatic steatosis and liver size
Looks for pneumonia or heart failure
supporting.only_if: respiratory symptoms, fever, or suspected heart failure

supporting.why: Excludes cardiac causes of edema and assesses function
supporting.only_if: suspected cardiac disease or edema out of proportion to hypoalbuminemia

not_indicated.why: No role unless pancreatitis is suspected
No role unless pancreatitis is suspected
No role in the evaluation of nutritional edema
Not routinely needed; only if cardiac ischemia is suspected
Not routinely needed; only if heart failure is suspected
Not routinely needed; only if heart failure is suspected

decision_points: Check glucose immediately; hypoglycemia is common and dangerous in young children
Correct hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and hypophosphatemia before and during refeeding to prevent refeeding syndrome
Treat or exclude infection (pneumonia, gastroenteritis, malaria, tuberculosis, HIV) before attributing all findings to malnutrition
Do not give large fluid boluses unless the child is in shock; edema is from hypoalbuminemia, not dehydration
Pregnancy test before imaging or teratogenic treatment in any postmenarchal female

criteria.name: Wellcome classification of protein-energy malnutrition
criteria.summary: Classifies malnutrition by weight-for-age and the presence of edema: kwashiorkor is edema with weight 60–80% of expected; marasmus is weight below 60% without edema; marasmic kwashiorkor is weight below 60% with edema.
items: Weight below 60% of expected without edema (marasmus)
Weight below 60% of expected with edema (marasmic kwashiorkor)

differential.name: Nephrotic syndrome
differential.why_considered: Generalized edema, hypoalbuminemia and poor growth in a young child
differential.trigger: Heavy proteinuria or periorbital edema that is worst in the morning

history: Edema that is worst on waking and shifts with posture
Recent upper respiratory infection or known glomerular disease
exam: Periorbital edema prominent, often with ascites and scrotal or vulvar edema
labs: Heavy proteinuria (3+ or more, or elevated urine protein-to-creatinine ratio)
Low albumin with normal total protein pattern dominated by protein loss

differential.name: Congestive heart failure
differential.why_considered: Edema, poor feeding, tachycardia and failure to thrive in an infant or child
differential.trigger: Tachycardia, hepatomegaly, cardiomegaly or a murmur

history: Poor exercise tolerance or cyanotic spells
exam: Tachycardia out of proportion to illness
Raised jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly, basal crackles
imaging: Cardiomegaly and pulmonary venous congestion on chest x-ray
Reduced systolic function or structural lesion on echocardiogram

differential.name: Protein-losing enteropathy
differential.why_considered: Hypoalbuminemia with edema and diarrhea in a child

history: Known inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease or prior cardiac surgery
exam: Abdominal distension without the hair and skin changes of kwashiorkor
labs: Low albumin with low total protein
imaging: Bowel wall thickening or abnormal small bowel on ultrasound or CT

differential.name: Chronic liver disease
differential.why_considered: Hypoalbuminemia, edema, abdominal distension and coagulopathy

history: Jaundice, easy bruising or gastrointestinal bleeding
Known hepatitis, metabolic liver disease or biliary disease
exam: Jaundice, spider angiomata, palmar erythema, caput medusae
Firm nodular liver edge or splenomegaly
labs: Prolonged PT and INR with thrombocytopenia
imaging: Nodular liver contour, splenomegaly and portal hypertension on ultrasound

differential.name: Marasmus
differential.why_considered: Severe wasting and growth failure from inadequate energy and protein intake

history: Severe global food deprivation rather than a starchy weaning diet
exam: Marked muscle wasting and loss of subcutaneous fat
No edema, no hair depigmentation, no peeling skin
labs: Albumin often normal or only mildly low

differential.name: Marasmic kwashiorkor
differential.why_considered: Both severe wasting and edema in the same child

history: Prolonged severe food deprivation followed by an acute stressor or infection
exam: Edema plus marked muscle wasting and loss of subcutaneous fat
Weight below 60% of expected for age
labs: Low albumin with severe electrolyte and glucose derangements

differential.name: Hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Poor growth, edema, dry skin and apathy in a child

history: Constipation, cold intolerance and prolonged jaundice in infancy
exam: Non-pitting myxedematous swelling, macroglossia, coarse facies
labs: Elevated TSH with low free T4

differential.name: Cystic fibrosis
differential.why_considered: Failure to thrive, hypoalbuminemia and edema from malabsorption

history: Recurrent respiratory infections, steatorrhea, salty-tasting skin
exam: Digital clubbing, nasal polyps, chronic cough
labs: Low albumin with fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies

severity.mild: Early edematous malnutrition: mild pitting edema of the feet, poor weight gain, irritability, and mild hypoalbuminemia without major electrolyte or glucose derangement.
severity.moderate: Established kwashiorkor: obvious pitting edema of legs, feet and face, sparse brittle depigmented hair, peeling hyperpigmented skin, apathy, and moderate hypoalbuminemia with hypokalemia or hypoglycemia.
severity.severe: Advanced disease: marked generalized edema, extensive skin desquamation, apathy or lethargy, severe hypoalbuminemia, and significant electrolyte, glucose and coagulation abnormalities.
severity.critical: Life-threatening: anasarca with shock, severe hypoglycemia, profound electrolyte derangement, or overwhelming concurrent infection such as sepsis, pneumonia or gastroenteritis.

red_flags.meaning: Severe hypoglycemia, sepsis or advanced metabolic derangement; needs immediate resuscitation
Common and dangerous in young children; treat immediately with glucose
Sepsis or severe dehydration; resuscitate cautiously because edema is not from fluid overload
Risk of arrhythmia and refeeding syndrome; correct before and during feeding

red_flags.finding: Extensive skin desquamation or weeping lesions
red_flags.meaning: Loss of skin barrier with risk of secondary infection and sepsis

red_flags.finding: Fever or focal signs of infection
red_flags.meaning: Concurrent infection is common and often precipitates presentation; treat or exclude it

complications.name: Refeeding syndrome
clues: Falling phosphate, potassium or magnesium after starting feeds

special_populations.differences: May present with failure to thrive and edema but less obvious hair and skin changes; hypoglycemia and hypothermia are more dangerous.
Classic presentation with growth retardation, hair depigmentation and peeling skin; growth charts are essential for assessment.
Rare, but can occur with severe protein restriction or malabsorption; edema and skin changes may be attributed to other causes and growth retardation is absent.
Edema may be attributed to normal pregnancy changes; nutritional assessment and fetal growth monitoring are important.
Higher risk of severe concurrent infection, which may be the presenting illness; a normal white count does not exclude infection.

key_questions.question: What has your child been eating and drinking over the past few weeks to months?
key_questions.looking_for: A diet dominated by starches or carbohydrates with very little protein, often after weaning from breast milk

key_questions.question: When did the swelling start, and where did it begin?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over weeks, starting in the feet and legs and spreading upward; pitting edema

key_questions.question: Has your child been growing and gaining weight normally?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor weight gain and growth failure despite the swelling

key_questions.question: Has there been any recent diarrhea, vomiting, fever, or illness?
key_questions.looking_for: A recent infection or diarrheal illness that precipitated the presentation

key_questions.question: How has your child's mood and behavior been?
Have you noticed any changes in your child's hair or skin?
key_questions.looking_for: Sparse, brittle, depigmented hair and dry, peeling, hyperpigmented skin

key_questions.question: Is your child still breastfeeding, and when did weaning occur?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent weaning onto a starchy, protein-poor diet

key_questions.question: Has your child had any trouble breathing, coughing, or fast breathing?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms of pneumonia or heart failure as alternative causes of edema

key_questions.question: Is there any history of heart, kidney, or liver disease in your child?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic conditions that could explain edema and hypoalbuminemia

key_questions.question: Does your child take any medications or supplements?
key_questions.looking_for: Medications that might affect appetite, growth, or fluid balance

key_questions.question: What is your family's access to food and clean water?
key_questions.looking_for: Food insecurity, poverty, displacement, or famine

key_questions.question: Has your child had any known exposure to tuberculosis, HIV, or other chronic infections?
key_questions.looking_for: Risk factors for concurrent infections that commonly complicate kwashiorkor

reasoning_points: Diet history of severe protein deficiency, often after weaning onto a starchy diet
Generalized pitting edema, typically starting in the feet and legs
Growth retardation with poor weight gain
Characteristic hair changes: sparse, brittle, depigmented hair
Characteristic skin changes: dry, peeling, hyperpigmented skin
Low total protein with electrolyte abnormalities such as hypokalemia and hypoglycemia
Exclusion of other causes of edema such as nephrotic syndrome, heart failure, and liver disease

easy: Toddler in a low-resource setting with classic pitting edema, hair depigmentation, and peeling skin
Clear history of weaning onto a protein-poor starchy diet
Marked hypoalbuminemia with low total protein
Growth retardation evident on growth chart
medium: Infant with failure to thrive and edema but less obvious hair and skin changes
Child with concurrent diarrheal illness or pneumonia obscuring the nutritional picture
Mild early disease with only pedal edema and poor weight gain
Coexisting iron deficiency anemia with microcytosis
hard: Older child or adolescent with severe protein restriction from an eating disorder or malabsorption
Edema attributed to heart failure or nephrotic syndrome until albumin and urine studies clarify
Marasmic kwashiorkor with both severe wasting and edema
Presentation with sepsis or severe hypoglycemia masking the underlying malnutrition
Normal or near-normal albumin early in the course despite classic clinical findings
